chapter-01.question: What makes a maintained source useful for multiple outputs?
options: The handbook, training material, and other outputs use the same maintained sources
Every output has the same layout
chapter-01.feedback: Reuse depends on explicit relationships and processing, not on a file format or platform.

chapter-01.question: Which statement best describes Document-as-Code?
options: Applying versioning, review and processing to maintained information
Publishing every file as a website
Using AI to write all procedures
chapter-01.feedback: The approach applies software-style discipline to information; it is not tied to one output or tool.

chapter-02.question: A contributor makes a Git commit. What is established by that action alone?
chapter-02.feedback: A commit records a revision. Review, automated checks and publication are separate.

chapter-02.question: Which tool records commits and branches?
chapter-02.feedback: Git is the version-control system; GitHub hosts Git repositories and adds collaboration tools.

chapter-03.question: Why record a source revision in a generated report?
options: To prove its content is approved
To connect the report to its inputs
chapter-03.feedback: A recorded revision supports provenance; it does not itself prove correctness.

chapter-03.question: An AI agent proposes changes to an access procedure and two related guides. What should reviewers examine?
options: Only the access procedure, because the guides cover the same topic
The diffs across all three files, checking that the instructions remain consistent
Only the agent's summary, because it describes the intended changes
Only the build results, because successful checks establish consistency
chapter-03.feedback: Review the actual changes across all affected files. A summary or successful build alone does not establish that the instructions remain consistent.

chapter-04.question: Which Markdown line creates a top-level heading?
chapter-04.feedback: A leading # followed by a space denotes a level-one heading.

chapter-04.question: Why can Markdown help with reviewing changes?
options: Its plain-text source can be compared in a diff
chapter-04.feedback: Text-based source can be inspected and compared; approval and reuse require other practices.

chapter-05.question: In a procedure file, what does 'owner: onboarding-team' describe?
options: The team that made the most recent edit
The team responsible for maintaining the procedure, not necessarily the team authorized to approve it
The team that approved the latest revision
The team responsible for running the validation program
chapter-05.feedback: The owner is responsible for maintaining the procedure. Who may approve it is a separate decision in the team's review process; ownership alone does not grant approval authority.

chapter-05.question: How do frontmatter and YAML relate in the procedure example?
options: Frontmatter checks the fields, while YAML approves the procedure
YAML is used only inside Markdown frontmatter
Frontmatter is the opening metadata block; YAML is the format used to write its fields
Frontmatter contains the instructions, while YAML controls their appearance
chapter-05.feedback: Frontmatter describes the block's position and purpose. YAML is a structured text format that can also be used in separate files.

chapter-05.question: You enter 'status: unknown' in the practice file and select Validate metadata. Why does the check fail?
options: The schema allows only draft or approved as status values
The source file must be committed before it can be checked
chapter-05.feedback: Unknown is valid text in YAML, but it is outside the status values allowed by this practice schema. The validator applies that rule when you run the check.

chapter-05.question: The practice file has 'status: draft' and passes validation. What does that result establish?
options: A reviewer has accepted the instructions
The instructions are accurate and safe to follow
The identifier is unique across the repository
The metadata satisfies the rules checked by the practice schema
chapter-05.feedback: A passing check confirms the configured metadata rules, including draft as an allowed status. It does not establish human approval, instruction accuracy, or cross-file identifier uniqueness.

chapter-06.question: Which item should remain identifiable if a procedure is renamed?
chapter-06.feedback: A stable identifier allows relationships to survive a title change.

chapter-06.question: If REQ-001 changes, the linked procedure PROC-001 must also be changed.
chapter-06.feedback: The relationship identifies PROC-001 as a candidate for review. A reviewer checks whether the revised requirement affects its instructions before deciding whether an edit is needed.

chapter-07.question: A successful processing run necessarily means the resulting handbook is approved.
chapter-07.feedback: Automated processing and human content approval are separate.

chapter-07.question: You edit the Contacts text and see the change in its preview, but the generated handbook still has the old wording. What updates the handbook?
options: Validate the Contacts metadata without rebuilding
Run checks and build successfully using the edited source
Change the Contacts status to approved without rebuilding
chapter-07.feedback: The preview follows the editor immediately. The handbook is a separate generated output: it changes after the configured checks pass and the build combines the current sources.

chapter-08.question: What is the distinction between a chat prompt and an AI agent?
options: A prompt gives instructions; an agent combines a model with tools whose access and actions depend on its configuration
A sufficiently detailed prompt gives the model access to the repository it names
An agent is simply a longer prompt containing more background information
chapter-08.feedback: A prompt describes the task; it does not grant access. An agent can retrieve sources or run checks through configured tools and permissions. A chat interface can also provide those tools: the distinction concerns the system's capabilities, not how its interface looks.

chapter-08.question: An agent updates a procedure and its build passes. What provides a basis for accepting the change?
options: The passing build alone establishes that the instructions are accurate
Reviewing the diff and generated outputs alongside the check results
The agent used versioned sources, so its changes need no further review
chapter-08.feedback: The build verifies configured processing, while the diff and outputs make the change inspectable. Reviewers use that evidence to assess meaning and suitability before acceptance.

chapter-09.question: What changes when you switch from a customer-focused view to a delivery-focused view of the same maintained records?
options: The records must be copied into a new source for each view
The selected information and its presentation change; the underlying records remain the same
The delivery relationships can be guessed from the record titles
chapter-09.feedback: Different questions select and present the same maintained information in different ways. Record identities and explicit relationships remain the source for each view.

chapter-09.question: AMD-001 is proposed and linked to DEL-101. DEL-102 depends on DEL-101. What does following these connections establish?
options: The amendment is effective and both deliveries must change
DEL-101 is directly linked, and DEL-102 is a candidate for review if the amendment is accepted
No review is useful until someone changes the delivery records
chapter-09.feedback: The recorded links support impact assessment. They do not make a proposed amendment effective or prove that every connected item needs an edit.

chapter-10.question: Which check can automatically detect a nonexistent activity reference?
chapter-10.feedback: A reference check can verify whether an identifier resolves.

chapter-10.question: A passing schema validation proves the owner is the right team.
chapter-10.feedback: It can confirm that an owner field exists, not its real-world correctness.

chapter-11.question: If a new build fails, what should remain available in a safe release process?
chapter-11.feedback: A failed build should not silently overwrite a working publication.

chapter-11.question: A source revision and a published edition always mean the same version.

chapter-12.question: What is the first question when two applications contain the same field?
chapter-12.feedback: Field ownership determines correct updates and conflict handling.

chapter-12.question: Exporting a diagram as an image always preserves its model relationships.
chapter-12.feedback: Visual appearance alone may not preserve object identities and links.

chapter-13.question: Which is a sensible first adoption target?
options: One useful output with accountable sources
chapter-13.feedback: A focused useful result permits early feedback and improvement.

chapter-13.question: Document-as-Code adoption can require changes to team responsibilities.
chapter-13.feedback: Maintaining rules, pipelines, and sources requires explicit ownership.
